title: Performance & Craft
description: Keep ray-marched shaders fast and precise.

lessons.title: Step count and precision
lessons.intro: Every shader in Act 2 has cost something, and none of the fifty-two stages before this one has reported what a pixel spent. Nothing in this sandbox measures work: iTime says what o'clock it is, not how long a fragment took, and there is no frame counter and no frame duration to ask for. What there is is the one number the march already holds: how many times round the loop it went before it stopped. Count that, hand it back through an out parameter, and paint it, and the cost of a picture becomes a picture. It will not give you milliseconds. It will tell you which pixels are doing the work, which is the question that actually decides what to change, and the answer is not the middle of the shape.
lessons.takeaway: A count is the only cost instrument this sandbox has, and it is enough to find the work. An out parameter carries it back without disturbing anything the march does, for one addition per iteration. The cheapest pixels are the couple of dozen aimed all but straight at the sphere, because their first sample already reports the whole distance to it and their second lands on the surface; the most expensive are the rays that pass just outside, creeping along the tangent in ever smaller steps until the loop bound stops them rather than the surface. A cyclic palette wraps, so the ceiling and the floor of a count share a colour and the ceiling has to be marked separately. Tightening the hit threshold buys accuracy at the silhouette and pays for it in steps at the silhouette, and loosening it does not blur the shape, it inflates it. Beneath both sits a floor set by the float itself. And the step budget is not free either: shrink it far enough and a t under twenty stops meaning a hit at all.
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, work out what the count at p of 0.525, 0.005 — a column three of the four common widths sample and the fourth does not — ought to be at a threshold of 0.03, given the 5 it reads at 0.05 and the 11 it reads at 0.01, then say why interpolating between two thresholds is not a sound way to guess. In the last stage, predict the budget at which the pixel at p.x of plus or minus 1 first joins the disc, given that it needs 8 steps to run out of distance.

stages.title: The count, painted
stages.body: steps is an out parameter: the march writes to it, the caller reads it, and nothing else about the loop changes. One addition per iteration is the whole cost of the instrument. Painted through Module 4's cosine palette, the frame comes back mostly red and orange with a thin ring of everything else through it. Read along the row at p.y of 0.005, the count is 2 in the middle and then 3, 4, 5 and 7 at p.x of 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 — the same five figures on the whole-hundredth columns a 371-pixel preview samples and on the half-hundredth columns the other three common widths sample, because out there the count is changing far too slowly for half a hundredth to matter. Two is as cheap as this scene gets, and it is arithmetic rather than luck: the first sample sits at the camera and reports 2.0, the entire distance to the sphere's near pole, so the second sample lands on the surface and the march is done. Going outward the background gets cheaper still — 8 steps at p.x of plus or minus 1, 7 at 1.2, and at the side edge itself 7 on the narrowest preview and 6 on the widest. Between the two is the ring, and it is steep. Swept along that row in twenty-thousandths, the count first reaches 12 at p.x of 0.48125, 24 at 0.52415, 48 at 0.53065 and 96 at 0.53095 — the last half of that climb inside three ten-thousandths of p. The colours climb with it: 0.854, 0.639, 0.020 at a count of 12, 0.500, 0.938, 0.062 at 24, 0.000, 0.741, 0.741 at 48 and 0.250, 0.241, 1.000 at 64. Averaged over the whole frame, a pixel costs 9.329 steps at 280 pixels across, 8.972 at 320, 8.559 at 371 and 7.981 at 480: the wider the preview, the more of it is cheap background.

stages.title: Where the count runs out
stages.body: The palette and the count disagree in exactly one place, and it is the place that matters. heat is a cosine, so heat of one and heat of zero are the same colour — 1.000, 0.259, 0.259 — which is very nearly the red the two-step pixels in the middle are already painted at 0.996, 0.318, 0.204. A march that spent its entire budget therefore looks like a march that spent almost none of it. One step against 95.5 separates them: the exhausted marches go white and everything else keeps its heat. There are 32 of them on a 280, 320 or 480-pixel preview and 24 on a 371-pixel one, and every one of those left the loop by running out of iterations rather than by passing a t of 20 — checked at all four of those widths in float and in double alike. They lie in a band between radii of 0.53106 and 0.53165, which is entirely outside this sphere and camera's true tangent radius of 0.53033: not one of them sits inside it, at any of the four widths, in either arithmetic. That is the character of the failure rather than an incidental fact about it. These are rays that miss, passing close enough that the field stays almost flat along them, so a grazing march can spend ninety-six steps without ever getting within a thousandth of anything. The expensive part is much wider than that white thread. 8,280 pixels cost twelve steps or more, and it is the same 8,280 at every one of those four widths, in both arithmetic models, and unmoved when every value map returns is nudged by a hundred-thousandth either way. 1,220 cost at least twenty-four, and 184 at least forty-eight — 1,196 and 182 respectively at 371. Set that against a disc of 8,888 pixels that the hit test accepts (8,882 at 371), of which 8,856 actually converged (8,858), and the shape of this shader's bill is plain: a rim a few pixels wide doing several times the work of everything it encloses.

stages.title: What tightening the threshold costs
stages.body: The hit threshold sweeps from a tenth down to a ten-thousandth and back every 15.71 seconds, and what it costs is not spread evenly over the frame. Read first on the half-hundredth grid three of the four common widths sample. At p of 0.005, 0.005 the count is 2 at every threshold in the sweep, because that ray's second sample already lands within a ten-thousandth of the surface and nothing in this range can force a third. At p of 0.205, 0.005 it runs 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5 and 5 across thresholds of 0.1, 0.05, 0.01, 0.003, 0.001, 0.0003 and 0.0001. At p of 0.405, 0.005 the same seven thresholds give 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10. At p of 0.505, 0.005: 4, 5, 8, 12, 15, 18 and 22. At p of 0.525, 0.005: 4, 5, 11, 18, 25, 33 and 40. Every one of those figures is identical in float and in double. A 371-pixel preview has none of those columns — it samples whole hundredths — and reading its own says something the table alone does not. p.x of 0 and 0.2 match 0.005 and 0.205 exactly; 0.4 comes back 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10, one short of 0.405 at the second-tightest threshold; and out at the rim the choice of column is most of the answer, with 0.52 giving 4, 5, 10, 15, 20, 26 and 31 and 0.53 giving 4, 6, 13, 23, 39, 64 and 93, and 0.525's row sitting between the two. The bill lands where the ray runs nearly parallel to the surface, which is the rim, every time. The other half of the trade is the shape. The furthest-out pixel that genuinely converges sits at a radius of 0.5906 at a threshold of 0.1, then 0.5602, 0.5361, 0.5320, 0.5305, 0.5303 and 0.5300 across the rest of the sweep on a 280, 320 or 480-pixel preview, and 0.5910, 0.5603, 0.5361, 0.5320, 0.5309, 0.5302 and 0.5300 on a 371-pixel one. The true tangent radius is 0.53033. A loose threshold does not soften the silhouette, it inflates it: at a tenth the disc is about eleven per cent too wide, because a march approaching almost side-on stops a tenth of a unit short of a surface it would have reached. Under all of this is a floor the render cannot cross. map here is a length of about one with one subtracted from it, and in the 32-bit float the driver runs, neighbouring values around one are between six and twelve hundred-millionths apart depending which side of one they fall. A threshold below that asks the subtraction for digits it has already thrown away, which is why this sweep stops where it does.

stages.title: A count is not a hit
stages.body: A loop bound has to be a compile-time constant, so a budget is spent by leaving early: if float(i) has reached it, break. The threshold is back at 0.001 and the only thing moving is how many steps are allowed, sweeping from 3 to 96 and back every 15.71 seconds. What is painted is the hit test's answer — heat where t came back under 20, background where it did not. Watch the background. At the full 96 steps, 8,888 pixels of a 280, 320 or 480-pixel preview pass that test and 8,856 of them genuinely reached the surface; on a 371-pixel preview it is 8,882 and 8,858. Cut the budget to 24 and the converged count falls to 8,628 while the number the test calls a hit climbs to 9,716. At 16 it is 8,208 against 11,248. At 12, 7,564 against 14,052. At 8, 5,924 against 28,244, which is already half the narrowest frame. At 6 the frame reads 98.59 per cent hits at 280 pixels across, 92.16 at 320, 79.49 at 371 and 61.44 at 480. At 5 every pixel of every one of those four widths reports a hit, while only 3,144 of them have touched anything at all — 3,156 at 371. The 371-pixel figures track the others within a few tens throughout. None of that is a fault in the picture. It is the hit test being asked a question it was never able to answer: t under 20 means the march did not run out of distance, and it has never meant the march arrived. Given a generous budget the two nearly coincide, which is why every stage since Module 8 has got away with the shorter test. Starve the loop and they come apart, and the sphere swallows the frame.

lessons.title: The cost of branching
lessons.intro: A branch reads as if it were free. One side runs, the other does not, and the work you skipped is work you did not pay for. On a processor that handles one pixel at a time that is exactly right. A GPU does not handle one pixel at a time: it runs a group of neighbouring pixels in lockstep, one instruction at a time for all of them, and when they disagree about which way a branch goes it runs both sides and discards the half each pixel did not ask for. So the price of a branch is not what it skipped. It is whether the pixels around it agreed. That is a real cost, and this module's instrument cannot measure it — but it can be made to show the thing that causes it.
lessons.takeaway: Writing a union as min or as an if produces the same field, the same march and the same count at every pixel, so the step counter cannot see a branch at all and no honest reading of this heatmap will tell you which form is dearer. What it can show is what makes branches expensive: disagreement between neighbours. Take the largest count in each two-by-two quad instead of each pixel's own and you have a model of what a lockstep group pays, and it is a model rather than a measurement — real hardware groups tens of pixels, not four, so this understates the effect rather than overstating it. Under that model the same work costs nearly twice as much scattered across the frame as it does gathered into blocks, with no change to any shape, to any threshold, or to the branch itself — and with the scattered arrangement never marching more pixels than the gathered one, within three per cent of the same number at every width. Coherence is the thing being bought, not the branch.
lessons.tryThis: In the last stage, work out what the coherent arrangement would cost under the quad model if the bands were two pixels wide instead of eight, and then say why that answer would be badly misleading about real hardware. In the third stage, say which pixels are raised by the quad maximum in a shader whose only branches belong to the march loop — its bound test and its two exits — and why the answer is about where the surface sits rather than about how map is written.

stages.title: A union, and what it costs
stages.body: Two shapes and a min: a ball of radius 0.55 at x of minus 0.6 and a cube of half-extent 0.45 at x of plus 0.6, both at a z of 3, painted by step count exactly as the last lesson painted the sphere. This is the baseline every stage in this lesson is measured against, so it is worth reading carefully. Along the row at p.y of 0.005 the count is 4 at p.x of minus 0.4, 2 at minus 0.3, 4 at minus 0.2 and 6 at minus 0.1, then 3, 3, 4 and 4 at plus 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4, 5 at 0.6 and 8 at plus or minus 1 — and each of those holds both on the whole-hundredth columns of a 371-pixel preview and on the half-hundredth columns the other three common widths sample, which is why they are the ones quoted. The 2 sits where the ray points straight at the ball's centre; the flat run of 3s and 4s across the cube is the front face, square-on to the camera, where the field hands back nearly the whole remaining distance on the first sample. The costly parts are the two outlines, and there the count is not stable enough to quote a pixel of: moving half a hundredth sideways at the ball's edge changes it by more than ten. Over the whole frame a pixel averages 8.196 steps at 280 pixels across, 7.928 at 320, 7.650 at 371 and 7.251 at 480, with 5,526 pixels passing the hit test at three of those widths and 5,476 at 371. Four marches exhaust their ninety-six steps at 280, 320 and 480, and two at 371 — and unlike the last lesson nothing marks them, so on that lesson's own warning they carry the same red as the two-step pixel at the ball's centre. Under the quad maximum in the third stage that becomes sixteen pixels, and eight at 371; across the last stage's two arrangements it is sixteen at most. The white marker is left out because this lesson's subject is elsewhere, and none of the eleven columns read off above is one of them — the dearest of those costs 8 steps.

stages.title: The same picture, with a branch in it
stages.body: map now chooses between the two distances with an if instead of a min. Nothing else in the shader has moved. The render is not merely similar to the last stage, it is the same: at all four common widths — 56,000, 64,000, 74,200 and 96,000 pixels — every pixel comes back with the identical step count and the identical t, and that holds in double arithmetic and under a full 32-bit float transcription alike. Not one pixel of 290,200 differs in either model. That is not a coincidence, it is what min is. Whenever the two distances differ, both forms pick the same one. When they are equal the two forms pick different operands — min hands back its first argument, the if falls through to its second — but the operands are equal, so the float that comes out is the same either way. The field is the same function written twice and the march cannot tell them apart. Which leaves the honest position, and it is worth stating plainly rather than working around. On real hardware these two are not the same instruction sequence, and a divergent branch genuinely costs more than a min. This heatmap counts iterations of a loop. It does not count instructions, it does not count the lanes that sat idle, and it has no clock behind it, so it cannot show you that difference and nothing in this sandbox can. What it can show is the condition that makes divergence expensive in the first place — neighbouring pixels that need different amounts of work — and that is what the next two stages measure. Notice also that the branch in this map is not per pixel at all. It is per sample, taken tens of times along every ray, and its two sides differ by one subtraction. A branch that cheap protects nothing worth protecting.

stages.title: What a group pays
stages.body: If a group of neighbouring pixels advances in lockstep, no member of it finishes before the slowest does. So march four rays instead of one — the two-by-two quad the current pixel belongs to, found by flooring fragCoord onto even coordinates — and paint the largest of the four counts. Every pixel in a quad then shows what the quad as a whole had to wait for. Against the last two stages the picture barely changes, and the numbers say why. The frame's total climbs from 458,952 steps to 478,120 at 280 pixels across, from 507,382 to 526,632 at 320, from 567,642 to 585,672 at 371 and from 696,084 to 715,488 at 480 — 4.18, 3.79, 3.18 and 2.79 per cent. Only 4,760 pixels are raised at all at 280, 4,842 at 320, 4,900 at 371 and 4,996 at 480, which is 8.50, 7.57, 6.60 and 5.20 per cent of each frame. Every one of those totals is identical in float and in double. Where it does bite it bites hard: the largest gap between a pixel's own count and its quad's worst is 83 steps at 280, 320 and 480, and 72 at 371. Those are the outlines. There is no branch in this map at all — it is back to a plain min — and the only branches left belong to the loop: its bound test and its two exits. Those exits are exactly what diverges here: a pixel that hits the ball squarely leaves the loop after a handful of trips while the one beside it grazes past and uses all ninety-six. That disagreement is in the geometry, not in how map is written, and no rewriting of map would remove it. Take the model for what it is. Four is the smallest group any GPU works in and real ones are far larger, so a genuine lockstep group would take its maximum over tens of pixels and these figures are a floor rather than an estimate.

stages.title: Gathered, and scattered
stages.body: Here is a branch that skips real work: about half the pixels march and the rest return a count of zero, painted as background. Which half is chosen two ways, alternating every 7.85 seconds — eight-pixel vertical bands, and a one-pixel checkerboard — and the picture is still the quad's worst count, so what you are looking at is what a lockstep group pays. Gathered into bands, whole quads never march and the frame goes dark in stripes: 51.43 per cent of it stays lit at 280 pixels across, 50.00 at 320 and 480 and 50.40 at 371. Scattered into a checkerboard, every quad contains a marching pixel and all of the frame lights up at all four widths, while marching within three per cent of the same number of pixels — 28,000 against the bands' 28,800 at 280, an exact 32,000 and 48,000 either way at 320 and 480, and 37,100 against 37,400 at 371. The totals under the model: 251,136 steps for the bands against 472,548 for the checkerboard at 280 pixels across, 267,896 against 521,048 at 320, 295,840 against 580,312 at 371 and 361,888 against 709,868 at 480 — factors of 1.88, 1.95, 1.96 and 1.96. The real work barely moved. Summed over the pixels that actually marched, the checkerboard does 229,476 steps against the bands' 238,566 at 280, 253,691 against 258,164 at 320, 283,821 against 285,652 at 371 and 348,042 against 352,070 at 480: in every one of those four cases the scattered arrangement does slightly less work and costs nearly twice as much. Nothing about the shapes changed, nothing about the threshold changed, and the branch itself is the same line of code both ways. What changed is whether neighbours agreed. That is the whole of what people mean when they say a branch is expensive, and it is why an early-out that fires in patches is worth having and one that fires per pixel is usually not.

lessons.title: Knowing when to stop
lessons.intro: Act 2 built one scene a piece at a time: a ray per pixel, a distance field to march it through, shapes joined and repeated, a normal read off the gradient, a light, a highlight, a shadow, fog and a sky for the fog to match. It is finished. The remaining question is not what else to add — there is always something else to add — but which of the things already there is earning what it costs. That is answerable now, because the count from the first two lessons can be pointed at the whole shader rather than the march alone, and every candidate cut can be priced and looked at side by side. Two cuts get made here. One is refused and one is taken, and the difference between them is measured rather than felt.
lessons.takeaway: Price a cut before making it, and look at it afterwards. Counted in calls to map, the finished frame averages about 25 or 26 per pixel depending on the preview's width, and about two thirds of what a lit pixel spends on lighting goes on the shadow ray rather than the normal. Dropping the shadow saves a fifth to a quarter of the whole frame and takes away the one thing that puts the ball on the ground rather than in front of it: refused. Reading the normal from four tetrahedral taps instead of six central differences saves between 3.5 and 4.2 per cent depending on the preview's width, and changes nothing an 8-bit display can show: taken. Neither of those is a rule. They are two measurements, and the judgement is what you do with them — which is a judgement, not an optimisation, and pretending otherwise is how shaders end up slower and worse at the same time. When the next cut costs something you can see, you have found the end.
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, work out roughly what share of the shadow ray's cost is spent on pixels whose colour does not change when it is removed, given that around 2,360 pixels change out of the 32,342 surface pixels a 320-pixel preview holds. Then in the last stage, decide whether you would take the four-tap normal into a scene full of hard corners, and name the one measurement that would settle it.

stages.title: The scene, finished
stages.body: Everything Act 2 built, running at once, with this module's counting march in place of the plain one. The counter itself is nearly free — one addition per iteration, and this stage ignores what it returns — but the swap is not, and a stage about pricing had better price its own change: Module 10's march ran sixty-four iterations and this one runs ninety-six, half as much loop again in the worst case. It moves pixels, too. 216 marches of a 280-pixel preview now run past sixty-four steps, 344 at 320, 632 at 371 and 1,624 at 480. Most of those come back with a t further along than Module 10's march ever reached — but not all of them, and the exception is worth having. A march that converges on its sixty-fifth step returns the t it already held after sixty-four increments, which is bit for bit what the shorter march returned when it ran out of iterations: 22 pixels at 280 land there, 40 at 320, 58 at 371 and 96 at 480, and they are exactly the ones the two versions agree on. Every other march that runs past sixty-four steps hands back something the shorter one never reached. None of this touches the colours quoted below. Those six pixels take 3, 5, 6, 21, 21 and 24 steps, so both marches stop at the same step on each of them and return the same t. A ball on a slab, a normal from six samples of the field, an ambient floor under a clamped cosine, a soft shadow folded into the diffuse term and the highlight both, the highlight mixed toward white rather than added, and fog over all of it against a sky whose horizon is the fog colour exactly. Reading it: on a preview an odd number of pixels across, where a column lands on p.x of zero, the ball is 0.259, 0.462, 0.542 at p.y of 0.005 and 0.299, 0.558, 0.656 at 0.205. On the half-hundredth columns the other three common widths sample, p of 0.205, 0.205 is 0.484, 0.721, 0.813, the slab at p of 0.605, minus 0.505 is 0.516, 0.563, 0.631, and the same point mirrored to minus 0.605, where the ball stands between it and the light, is 0.368, 0.412, 0.469 — a shadow you can still read the ground through. Nothing clips: the brightest channel anywhere in the frame is 0.9183, inside the highlight, and it is 0.9183 at every one of the four common widths in both float and double arithmetic, with no pixel of any of those frames exceeding one in any channel. This is the thing to be judged. It looks finished, and looking finished is not evidence about anything except how it looks.

stages.title: What it costs
stages.body: The same scene, painted by what it spends. Every call to map is counted: the primary march reports its own, the shadow march reports its own, and the normal's six are added as a constant because six is what a central difference always costs. The total divides by 160 rather than 96, since the ceiling here is ninety-six plus six plus forty-eight, and 160 keeps the most expensive pixel short of the palette's wrap. A pixel averages 25.221 calls at 280 pixels across, 25.326 at 320, 25.578 at 371 and 26.456 at 480. The split is the surprise. A pixel that hits something spends 6 on its normal and, on average, 11.9 calls at 280 and 320, 11.8 at 371 and 11.7 at 480 on the shadow ray alone, against 18.5, 19.5, 20.9 and 23.7 on the primary march. Two thirds of what a lit pixel spends on lighting is a second march nobody sees — 66.5, 66.4, 66.3 and 66.1 per cent of the normal and the shadow taken together, across those same four widths. Read the colours: the ball at p of 0, 0.005 and 0, 0.205, and at p of 0.205, 0.205, all cost 22 calls and all paint 0.825, 0.677, 0.010, and each of those readings survives moving the sampling column half a hundredth either way, so no preview width disagrees. The slab at p of 0.605, minus 0.505 costs 38 and paints 0.539, 0.918, 0.044; the shadowed point at minus 0.605, minus 0.505 costs 36 and paints 0.578, 0.895, 0.030 — a shadowed pixel is cheaper than a lit one, because its shadow ray stops the moment it meets the ball. The worst pixel in the frame reaches the full 150 at 280, 320 and 480 and 130 at 371, and between 47.19 and 51.97 per cent of the frame hits something at all, depending on the width. Those are the numbers a cut has to beat.

stages.title: The cut that is refused
stages.body: The shadow ray is the single biggest line in the bill, so it is the first thing anyone reaches for. Here it is switched on and off every 7.85 seconds by a value derived from iTime, which makes it the coherent branch the last lesson argued for: every pixel in the frame takes the same side, so the cheap half of the cycle is genuinely cheap rather than nominally cheap. It saves a great deal. The frame's average falls from 25.22 calls a pixel to 19.03 at 280 pixels across, 25.33 to 19.33 at 320, 25.58 to 19.78 at 371 and 26.46 to 20.94 at 480 — 24.54, 23.68, 22.68 and 20.85 per cent of everything the shader does. And it takes away almost nothing, if you count pixels. 2,360 of them change by more than half a level of 255 at 280, 320 and 480, and 2,370 at 371 — 4.21, 3.69, 3.19 and 2.46 per cent of those frames, and the same counts in double arithmetic and under a 32-bit float transcription both. The largest single change is 0.2184, at p of minus 0.145, minus 0.615 on the half-hundredth grid and minus 0.15, minus 0.615 on the whole-hundredth one. But look at where those two thousand pixels are. The point at p of minus 0.605, minus 0.505 goes from 0.368, 0.412, 0.469 to 0.516, 0.563, 0.631 — identical, now, to its mirror image on the lit side, so the ball no longer casts anything. The slab directly under the ball at p of 0, minus 0.605 goes from 0.426, 0.461, 0.513 to 0.482, 0.518, 0.574. Two per cent of the pixels were carrying the entire claim that the ball is resting on the slab rather than floating in front of it. A quarter of the cost for the one cue that makes the scene a scene is a bad trade, and this cut is refused.

stages.title: The cut that is taken, and the end
stages.body: The normal is the other repeated cost, and it has a cheaper form. Instead of six samples in central-difference pairs, take four at the corners of a tetrahedron and add them up weighted by their own offsets: k.xyy, k.yyx, k.yxy and k.xxx built from a vec2 of plus and minus one give the four directions, and the sum points the same way the gradient does. Two fewer calls to map on every pixel that hits something. The saving is small and real: the frame average falls from 25.22 calls a pixel to 24.18 at 280 pixels across, 25.33 to 24.32 at 320, 25.58 to 24.59 at 371 and 26.46 to 25.51 at 480, which is 4.12, 3.99, 3.84 and 3.57 per cent. What it costs is nothing you can display. Across all four of those widths, in double arithmetic and under a full 32-bit float transcription both, not a single pixel changes by as much as half a level of 255; the largest change anywhere is 0.00075 in double arithmetic and under nine ten-thousandths in float, which is still under a quarter of one level. Every figure quoted in the first stage comes back unchanged to three decimals except p of 0.205, 0.205, which moves from 0.484, 0.721, 0.813 to 0.485, 0.721, 0.813. Nothing clips, and the brightest channel is still 0.9183. So this cut is taken and the scene is done. Not because there is nothing left to try — a bounding test, a coarser far field, a cheaper fog — but because the next thing on the list would have to be measured the same way, and the moment a cut starts costing something a display can show, the answer stops being arithmetic and starts being taste. Knowing that the line is there, and that it is yours to draw rather than a number's, is the last thing Act 2 has to teach.
